name: Chordoid glioma of the third ventricle
aliases: chordoid glioma of the third ventricle

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A rare, slow-growing glial tumour (CNS WHO grade 2) arising characteristically in the anterior third ventricle of adults, more often women
Its location near the hypothalamus and optic pathways produces visual disturbance, endocrine and hypothalamic dysfunction, and features of raised intracranial pressure
MRI typically shows a well-circumscribed, ovoid, homogeneously enhancing suprasellar/third-ventricular mass
A recurrent PRKCA gene mutation is highly characteristic and aids molecular diagnosis
Histology shows cords and clusters of epithelioid glial cells in a mucinous, chordoid matrix with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate
The tumour is GFAP-positive, confirming its glial nature
Complete resection is desirable but often difficult owing to adherence to critical hypothalamic structures
reference.pathophysiology: Chordoid glioma is a rare, low-grade glial tumour that arises in the anterior third ventricle, probably from specialised ependymal or tanycyte-like cells of the region near the lamina terminalis. It grows as a circumscribed mass composed of cords and nests of epithelioid, glial-fibrillary-acidic-protein-positive cells embedded in a mucinous, chordoid stroma, typically accompanied by a lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate. A recurrent activating mutation of the PRKCA gene is a defining molecular feature. Although histologically low grade and slow-growing, its intimate relationship with the hypothalamus, optic chiasm and cerebrospinal fluid pathways makes it clinically significant and surgically challenging.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the third-ventricular/suprasellar mass
Formal visual field and acuity assessment for chiasmal compression
Anterior pituitary and hypothalamic endocrine evaluation
Histopathology showing epithelioid glial cords in a chordoid, mucinous matrix
GFAP immunohistochemistry to confirm glial origin
PRKCA molecular testing to support the diagnosis
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss from chiasmal compression
Hypothalamic dysfunction such as disordered temperature, appetite or consciousness
Obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
Postoperative hypothalamic injury causing endocrine and autonomic instability
reference.prognosis: As a low-grade tumour, prognosis after complete resection is favourable, but its deep location adjacent to the hypothalamus frequently prevents total removal, leading to recurrence and significant surgical morbidity. Subtotally resected tumours may be managed with adjuvant radiotherapy, and long-term endocrine and visual sequelae are common.
pitfalls: Confusing it with craniopharyngioma or meningioma and misjudging the surgical approach
Attempting radical resection at the cost of severe hypothalamic injury
Underestimating perioperative endocrine and hypothalamic complications
Not considering PRKCA testing to confirm an uncertain diagnosis
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Maximal safe surgical resection is the primary and generally only established treatment, aiming for gross total removal when feasible without unacceptable risk to the hypothalamus and optic apparatus
Surgery also provides diagnostic tissue for histology and PRKCA mutation testing
A transcallosal or transcortical approach is typically used to access the third ventricle, but the deep location often limits complete resection and carries risk of hypothalamic and endocrine injury
Adjuvant radiotherapy (fractionated external beam or stereotactic radiosurgery) is considered when resection is subtotal or tumour is left in situ due to hypothalamic adherence
Radiotherapy is also used at recurrence or on further growth of residual disease, rather than routinely after complete resection
There is no established role for cytotoxic chemotherapy or targeted systemic therapy in this tumour
For recurrent disease, options are re-resection where feasible or radiotherapy if not already given, decided within a neuro-oncology or skull base multidisciplinary team
In unresectable or high-risk lesions in poor surgical candidates, a more conservative approach of biopsy plus radiotherapy or close observation with serial imaging may be considered
Surveillance brain MRI at intervals to detect recurrence or progression of residual tumour
Serial formal visual field and visual acuity assessment given proximity to the optic chiasm
Ongoing anterior pituitary and hypothalamic endocrine evaluation, since hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction including diabetes insipidus is common and may evolve over time
Clinical monitoring for signs of raised intracranial pressure or recurrent hydrocephalus given the tumour's potential to obstruct CSF flow
Prompt referral to a neurosurgical service with third-ventricular and skull base experience, ideally within a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team
Referral to endocrinology, radiation oncology, and ophthalmology as appropriate for perioperative endocrine management, adjuvant or salvage radiotherapy, and visual surveillance
